chunks.title: Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.section: Cleaning and dressing a minor wound
chunks.text: Wash your hands first if water is available. Irrigate the wound with clean drinking water under pressure — a plastic bottle with a pinhole in the cap works well. Aim for at least 250 ml for a small wound. Do not use hydrogen peroxide or undiluted antiseptic inside an open wound. Both damage healing tissue and slow recovery. Remove visible grit with clean tweezers. Pat dry, apply a thin layer of antibiotic ointment if available, and cover with a sterile non-adherent dressing. Change the dressing daily, or sooner if it becomes wet or dirty.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain first aid guidance (WHO/ICRC field manuals)

chunks.title: Breathing and Cardiac Emergencies
chunks.text: Check for danger, then check for a response by shouting and squeezing the shoulders. If there is no response, shout for help and open the airway by tilting the head back and lifting the chin. Look, listen, and feel for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds. Occasional gasping is not normal breathing and is a sign of cardiac arrest. If breathing is absent or abnormal, begin chest compressions. Place the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, the other hand on top, and interlock the fingers. Compress hard and fast: 5 to 6 cm deep, at 100 to 120 compressions per minute. Allow the chest to recoil fully between compressions. Give 30 compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths. If you are unwilling or unable to give breaths, continuous compressions alone are far better than nothing. Swap rescuers every two minutes if possible, because compression quality falls sharply with fatigue. Continue until the person shows signs of life, a defibrillator is ready to use, or you are physically unable to continue.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain resuscitation council guidance

chunks.title: Breathing and Cardiac Emergencies
chunks.text: Typical symptoms are central crushing chest pain or pressure lasting more than a few minutes, often spreading to the jaw, neck, or left arm, with sweating, nausea, and shortness of breath. Women, older adults, and people with diabetes more often present without classic chest pain — instead with sudden fatigue, breathlessness, or indigestion-like discomfort. Sit the person down, leaning back with knees bent. This position reduces the workload on the heart. If they are not allergic and not already bleeding, give one 300 mg aspirin and ask them to chew it slowly. Chewing gets it into the bloodstream faster than swallowing. Do not let them walk to transport. Exertion during a heart attack can trigger cardiac arrest.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain resuscitation council guidance

chunks.title: Environmental Emergencies
chunks.text: Never give alcohol, which dilates skin vessels and accelerates heat loss. Handle a severely hypothermic person gently and keep them horizontal. Rough handling can trigger a fatal heart rhythm. Do not rub the limbs or place them in hot water. Rewarming the limbs first drives cold blood back to the core and can drop the core temperature further.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain wilderness medicine guidance

chunks.title: Environmental Emergencies
chunks.text: Early dehydration shows as thirst, dark urine, and reduced urine output. Later signs are dizziness on standing, a fast pulse, sunken eyes, and skin that stays tented when pinched. An oral rehydration solution can be mixed from six level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt in one litre of clean water. Getting the proportions right matters: too much sugar worsens diarrhoea. Give small sips frequently rather than large volumes at once, which usually causes vomiting. Aim for a cup after each loose stool. A person who cannot keep fluids down, or who has stopped passing urine for more than eight hours, needs intravenous fluids.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain wilderness medicine guidance

chunks.title: Trauma and Sudden Collapse
chunks.text: Suspect a spinal injury after any fall from height, a diving accident, a vehicle collision, or any injury with head trauma and altered consciousness. Symptoms include neck or back pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in the limbs, and loss of bladder control. Keep the head, neck, and spine in a straight line. Hold the head still with both hands and tell the person not to move. Do not move the person unless they are in immediate danger, such as fire or rising water. If you must move them, use a log roll with several people keeping the spine aligned as a single unit. If the person is unconscious and breathing but you must leave them, place them in the recovery position while keeping the spine as aligned as possible. A protected airway takes priority over a perfectly immobilised spine.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain emergency care guidance

chunks.title: Trauma and Sudden Collapse
chunks.text: Do not restrain the person and do not put anything in their mouth. Swallowing the tongue is a myth; forcing objects into the mouth breaks teeth and blocks the airway. Clear hard objects away, cushion the head, and note the time the seizure started. Once the convulsion stops, roll the person into the recovery position and allow them to sleep. Confusion and drowsiness afterwards are normal and can last an hour. Call for emergency help if the seizure lasts more than five minutes, if a second seizure follows without full recovery, if it is the person's first seizure, if they are injured, pregnant, or diabetic, or if the seizure occurred in water.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain emergency care guidance

chunks.title: Burns and Poisoning
chunks.text: Superficial burns are red and painful with no blisters, and heal in about a week. Partial thickness burns are blistered, wet, and intensely painful. Full thickness burns look white, brown, or charred and leathery, and may be painless because the nerve endings are destroyed. Painlessness is a sign of a worse burn, not a milder one. Estimate the burned area using the person's own palm including fingers as roughly one percent of their body surface. Seek urgent care for any burn larger than the person's palm, any full thickness burn, any burn to the face, hands, feet, genitals, or across a joint, and any burn that encircles a limb or the chest.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain emergency care guidance

chunks.title: Burns and Poisoning
chunks.text: Do not induce vomiting. It causes further damage on the way back up, particularly with corrosives and petroleum products, and risks fluid entering the lungs. Identify what was taken, how much, and when. Keep the container, packaging, or plant sample for the medical team. If the substance is corrosive and the person is fully alert, small sips of water or milk can dilute it. Give nothing by mouth to a drowsy person. For skin contact, remove contaminated clothing and wash the skin with copious water for at least 15 minutes. For eye contact, irrigate the open eye with clean water for at least 20 minutes, sweeping from the inner corner outward. If the person becomes unresponsive but is breathing, place them in the recovery position, because vomiting is common in poisoning.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain emergency care guidance

chunks.title: Disaster Response and Survival
chunks.text: Shelter is the priority ahead of water and food in cold or wet conditions, because exposure kills in hours rather than days. Choose a site out of the wind, off the valley floor where cold air pools, away from dead trees and rockfall, and above any possible flood line. Insulate underneath before building anything overhead. Dry leaves, grass, or a pack beneath the body prevents the ground conducting away body heat. Keep the shelter small. A space just large enough for your body is warmed by your body; a large shelter is not. Keep clothing dry and avoid sweating. Wet insulation loses most of its value, so remove layers before working hard and replace them immediately afterward.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain civil defence and survival guidance

chunks.title: Disaster Response and Survival
chunks.text: Move to high ground immediately and do not wait for instructions if water is rising. Do not walk through moving water. Fifteen centimetres of moving water can knock an adult off their feet, and the surface hides washed-out ground. Do not drive through floodwater. Sixty centimetres of water floats most vehicles, and most flood deaths involve vehicles. Assume all floodwater is contaminated with sewage, fuel, and debris. Wash thoroughly after any contact and cover wounds. Electricity and standing water are lethal together. Do not enter a flooded room where the power may still be on. After a flood, discard any food that has touched floodwater, and do not drink tap water until authorities declare it safe.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain civil defence and survival guidance
